hints: Focus on finding a chiral carbon, a carbon joined to four completely different atoms or groups.
Look closely at compound 1, the middle carbons each carry H, OH and two different chain ends above and below.
Check compound 3 for symmetry and planarity around the C=C bond, then decide which combination of 1 and 2 only leaves you with.
walkthrough:
**Recall the test for optical isomerism**

A molecule shows optical isomerism if it has at least one chiral centre and no internal compensation. A chiral centre is a carbon with four different groups attached.

Rule: $\text{chiral C = C attached to 4 different groups}$

**Analyse compound 1**

This is an aldopentose, $\text{HOCH}_2\text{(CHOH)}_3\text{CHO}$. Look at the three middle $\text{CH(OH)}$ carbons.

Each one is bonded to $\text{H}$, $\text{OH}$, a chain going up toward $\text{CHO}$ and a different chain going down toward $\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$. All four groups are different, so compound 1 has three chiral centres and definitely has optical isomers.

**Analyse compound 2**

This is a substituted cyclohexane with $\text{OH}$, $\text{CH(CH}_3)_2$ and $\text{CH}_3$ on carbons 1, 2 and 4.

Each of those ring carbons is bonded to $\text{H}$, its substituent, and two different ring paths clockwise and anticlockwise. Because the substituents break the symmetry, these are chiral centres, so compound 2 also has optical isomers.

**Analyse compound 3**

Compound 3 is $\text{HOOC-CH=CH-COOH}$, the trans diacid.

The $\text{C=C}$ carbons each have only three groups and are planar, so they cannot be chiral. The molecule is flat and achiral, it shows cis-trans isomerism but not optical isomerism. Therefore only 1 and 2 qualify.

options.A: Incorrect. This suggests 1, 2 and 3 all have optical isomers. Compounds 1 and 2 do, but 3 is planar around C=C with no carbon bearing four different groups, so it cannot be optically active.
options.B: Correct. Compound 1 has three chiral CH(OH) centres and compound 2 has chiral ring carbons bearing OH, isopropyl and methyl groups. Compound 3 has no chiral centre, so only 1 and 2 show optical isomerism.
options.C: Incorrect. This suggests 2 and 3 only. While 2 is correctly included, 3 is wrongly included and 1 is wrongly left out. Compound 1 clearly has multiple chiral centres, and compound 3 has none.
options.D: Incorrect. This suggests 1 only. Compound 1 is indeed optically active, but compound 2 is also optically active because its three substituted ring carbons are chiral. You must include both 1 and 2.
